Suncoast burn bans lifted
WWSB ABC7 News at 5pm
By Megan Kennedy
Published: Apr. 15, 2026 at 5:26 PM EDT
Share
Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google
SARASOTA, Fla. (WWSB) - Dry conditions have consumed our state for the last sis months and brush and wild fires have been prevalent...
One of the most recent fires being in Collier County where I-75 converges with Alligator Alley. More than 1,700 acres have burned with the blaze being 70% contained at our latest update.
Now, Sarasota county has dropped the burn bans despite the Suncoast still being in an extreme drought.
Manatee lifted their burn ban on March 20th.
They too are advising caution when burning.
Even though burning is now allowed, county officials are urging the community to practice extreme caution.
The Keetch Byram Drought Index measures the water content in our soil. The higher the number, the drier the ground.
This is a tool that the local fire departments use daily.
Officials with Sarasota county tell us that if the levels drop below 500 for a week straight, then the ban can be lifted.
However Sarasota County Fire Department officials say that even though the drought is lifted, it doesn’t mean that we can drop our guard.
“It doesn’t mean that all the conditions are right and we can just go out and we can do whatever we need to do because we still have heat, we still have wind, and we still have low humidity. So all of those things play into the prevalence of starting a brush fire or a wildland fire.
So even though we’re out of a burn ban it doesnt mean we can lower our state height of awareness and out height of awareness. We need to maintain height of awareness.”-Explains Sarasota County Fire Department Assistant Fire Chief, Tim Dorsey
Dorsey continued by saying as soon as the KBDI does above 500, the burn ban will be reinstated.

Suncoast metro area ranks 15th deadliest in nation for pedestrian fatalities
WWSB ABC7 News at 6:30pm
By Natalia Kaminski and Noah Chase
Published: Jun. 20, 2026 at 4:16 PM EDT
Share
Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google
SARASOTA, Fla.
(WWSB) - The North Port-Bradenton-Sarasota metro area now ranks 15th deadliest in the nation for pedestrian fatalities, according to Smart Growth America’s “Dangerous by Design” report .
The ranking marks a troubling trend for the region, which has climbed from 19th in 2022 and 17th in 2024.
The report, which ranks all 50 states and the largest 101 metro areas by pedestrian fatality rates, found 153 people were killed while walking in the Suncoast region between 2020 and 2024.
“Any pedestrian fatality is one too many and most of these fatalities are fully preventable,” said Meredith Censullo of the Bradenton Police Department.
Not all residents share alarm over the report’s findings. Sarasota residents Cynthia Barta and Cathryn Cooper said walking downtown feels safe, outside of a few close calls.
“In general, it’s pretty much safe but there’s a few corners that I’ve had issues one when I have been in the middle of the crosswalk and almost hit because people don’t stop completely,” Barta said.
Caught on Camera: Red-light runner misses collision on U.S. 301 by inches
Cooper said she sees accidents that could be avoided by following basic pedestrian laws.
“Instead of looking they will just step right off the curb and like wow you didn’t even look,” Cooper said.
Data from the Sarasota-Manatee Metropolitan Planning Organization shows 11 of the 12 pedestrian deaths in the city of Bradenton between 2020 and 2024 happened at night.
“Not using an intersection not in a crosswalk so those are those conditions that are going to be dangerous,” Censullo said.
Censullo encourages both pedestrians and drivers to stay alert.
Multiple Suncoast traffic units say they are working on adding signage, keeping drivers aware, and educating pedestrians on safety.
The Bradenton-Sarasota-North Port metro area is not alone.
According to the report, six Florida metros made the top 20 deadliest list, more than any other state in the country. Overall, Florida is ranked fifth in the nation for pedestrian fatalities.
